papers.title: mmPoison: Targeted Clean-label Poisoning Attacks on mmWave-based Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Nowadays, mmWave-based human activity recognition (HAR) systems are widely used in smart homes, healthcare monitoring, and telemedicine. To achieve high accuracy, HAR systems require large-scale data collection from distributed sources for model training, such as edge devices or public repositories, which opens up opportunities for attackers to inject poisoned data into the training process, inducing false predictions and damaging the reliability of mmWave-based HAR systems. This paper presents targeted clean-label poisoning attack strategies, mmPoison, which injects imperceptible poisoned data into the training datasets for causing misclassifications on target instances in mmWave-based HAR systems without controlling the labeling process. In mmPoison, different attack methodologies are proposed for different attacker capabilities. For white-box setting, discriminative region masking is used to limit perturbations in discriminative regions. Then, mmPoison updates perturbations based on parameter trajectory alignment, and optimizes the poisoned instances to remain close to the clean instances. This process is iteratively applied to generate poisoned datasets. For black-box setting, mmPoison trains surrogate models with pseudo-label supervision and then uses them in a generator-discriminator framework to generate poisoned instances by jointly optimizing attack effectiveness and imperceptibility. Experiments conducted on public and self-collected datasets validate the effectiveness and imperceptibility of mmPoison in causing misclassifications within mmWave-based HAR systems.

papers.title: Sharing of Irreversible Latent Features in lieu of RF IQ Data for Multiple Downstream Learning Tasks
papers.abstract: Wireless in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) data is useful for training various radio frequency (RF) machine learning (ML) models. However, sharing such I/Q data faces barriers from concerns of (i) potentially violating laws related to recording raw samples that can eventually be decoded by an unauthorized third party, and (ii) revealing information about a proprietary system or the environment involved in the data capture. This paper proposes a different solution to sharing I/Q data intended for use in ML models by leveraging latent embeddings obtained through a shared encoder. The key contributions include: (i) demonstrating how a single set of common features can be extracted from an I/Q dataset for training multiple downstream RF classification or regression tasks, (ii) designing a method of structured noise infusion that impairs the reverse recovery of the raw I/Q from the feature space without significant impact to the downstream tasks, and (iii) demonstrating the application of this method on informative real-world, publicly available datasets. Sharing well-constructed yet privacy-preserving features can accelerate foundational research on ML for wireless without relying on hard-to-get I/Q samples.

papers.title: Continuous Passive Target Tracking over Intermittent and Narrow Sensing Beams in 6G Networks
papers.abstract: 6G networks promise an advanced infrastructure for high-precision passive sensing and tracking, particularly in emerging sectors like Low-Altitude Economy (LAE) and Internet of Vehicles. However, realizing passive sensing in 6G remains challenging due to its unique signal characteristics, especially the extreme directionality of narrow beams and the intermittent availability of sensing resources, which are subordinated to the primary communication traffic. In this paper, we propose SPOT, a novel passive beam tracking framework that achieves continuous, high-precision tracking using only temporally sparse sensing slots. We employ an Interacting Multiple Model combined with an Extended Kalman Filter (IMM-EKF) to robustly predict non-linear target dynamics. We further develop a beam selection strategy that maximizes Fisher information gain to minimize tracking uncertainty, integrated with an opportunistic exploration mechanism to detect emerging targets. To reduce computation complexity, we introduce a lightweight approximation of the Posterior Cramér-Rao Lower Bound. Extensive evaluations using both simulations and real-world datasets demonstrate that SPOT significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving a detection rate near 100% and an average tracking error below 1 meter, even in multi-target scenarios with highly sparse temporal updates.

papers.title: Efficient Secure Federated Learning via Information-Theoretically Secure Key Distribution: A Medical Imaging Case Study
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of models across institutions without centralizing sensitive data, making it well-suited for privacy-concerned applications, such as medical imaging. To protect FL model updates during secure aggregation, additive masking is commonly employed. However, its underlying classical key establishment is only computationally secure. On the other hand, physics-based Information-Theoretically Secure (ITS) key exchange introduces practical constraints: finite key generation rates and time-limited storage severely limit throughput and sustained training of uncompressed models. In this work, we address this bottleneck by developing an FL framework that integrates frozen backbones, knowledge distillation, and quantization. These techniques reduce communication payload and, consequently, key material consumption. Moving beyond simulation, we benchmark this framework on a real physics-based key distribution testbed involving a chest X-ray classification application. Our results show that key usage can be reduced by ~35× while maintaining predictive accuracy. This prevents buffer depletion and key expiration, enabling sustainable FL training under physical key generation constraints.

papers.title: Over-the-Air Federated Learning in Heterogeneous Mobile Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: Over-the-air computation has emerged as a scalable and efficient solution for deploying federated learning algorithms in wireless networks by exploiting waveform superposition for simultaneous model aggregation. Most existing work struggles with heterogeneous fading channels. These approaches either enforce unbiased updates from all devices or allow partial device contributions, requiring careful tuning of the convergence bound to mitigate bias under specific fading models. However, the former significantly amplifies receiver noise due to the weakest channel, whereas the latter is sensitive to fading model mismatch and converges only to a biased objective. To tackle these challenges, we propose FedOAG, which employs algorithmic components to automatically satisfy energy constraints via gradient normalization and evenly mix devices' updates through implicit gossiping. Importantly, FedOAG does not require transmission from all devices, nor does it rely on a specific fading model or knowledge of time-varying statistical channel distributions. We show that FedOAG converges to a stationary point of an unbiased non-convex objective at the best possible rate O(1/T) for any stochastic first-order method. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments over dynamic wireless conditions on real-world datasets.

papers.title: S kynet : Workflow-Level Anomaly Detection for Agentic AI via Semantic and Structural Modeling
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems execute complex tasks through long-horizon workflows of planning, tool use, and multi-agent coordination. Task failures in these systems often originate from a single step, such as an injected prompt or a flawed plan, and are then amplified through downstream dependencies as the corrupted step propagates across many subsequent agents and tool calls. Existing defenses either target a specific class of attacks or failures, or inspect individual prompts and steps in isolation. Both leave the global dependency structure of a workflow unexamined, and miss the inconsistencies that only emerge when the execution is viewed as a whole. We argue that anomaly detection for agentic AI must reason at the workflow level, where global execution structure exposes signals that local checks cannot see. We present Skynet, a principled workflow-level anomaly detection framework that turns observed multi-agent execution into directed workflow graphs and scores them against learned benign behavior. Skynet jointly models the semantic execution context and the structural organization of inter-agent delegation, tool invocation, and data-flow dependencies, and trains only on benign workflows. Because training never sees attacks or failures, this design naturally extends to zero-day detection: any execution that violates benign workflow regularities surfaces as off-manifold geometry under a single decision rule. We evaluate Skynet on three public agentic safety and failure benchmarks. It sustains high recall together with a sub-1% false positive rate, with per-workflow and per-step latencies low enough for online monitoring of agentic AI runtimes.

papers.title: Just Talk Once: Communication-Efficient Split Federated LLM Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is increasingly shifting toward data generated on edge devices, where memory, computation, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints make conventional federated learning difficult to sustain. Split federated fine-tuning (SFT) improves client-side efficiency by offloading most model parameters and computation to the server but requires step-by-step bidirectional communication loop across the split interface and forces continuous client involvement throughout training. In this paper, we present L-shaped SFT, a split fine-tuning framework that removes this bidirectional bottleneck. Our key insight is that weight tying in modern LLMs enables server-side hidden activations to be directly supervised using target embeddings, allowing the training loss to be computed on the server without returning server outputs to the client. To further eliminate the need for continuous client participation, based on L-shaped SFT, we introduce one-shot SFT, in which clients upload activations once and then go offline while the server continues optimization over cached representations. We implement our design in a real system testbed with heterogeneous edge clients, including commercial smartphones and NVIDIA developer boards. Experiments demonstrate that our schemes significantly reduce communication costs and client online time compared with existing SFT baselines.

papers.title: Optimizing Stochastic Gradient Push under Broadcast Communications
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the convergence time for decentralized federated learning (DFL) in wireless networks under broadcast communications, with focus on mixing matrix design. The mixing matrix is a critical hyperparameter for DFL that simultaneously controls the convergence rate across iterations and the communication demand per iteration, both strongly influencing the convergence time. Although the problem has been studied previously, existing solutions are mostly designed for decentralized parallel stochastic gradient descent (D-PSGD), which requires the mixing matrix to be symmetric and doubly stochastic. These constraints confine the activated communication graph to undirected (i.e., bidirected) graphs, which limits design flexibility. In contrast, we consider mixing matrix design for stochastic gradient push (SGP), which allows asymmetric mixing matrices and hence directed communication graphs. By analyzing how the convergence rate of SGP depends on the mixing matrices, we extract an objective function that explicitly depends on graph-theoretic parameters of the activated communication graph, based on which we develop an efficient design algorithm with performance guarantees. Our evaluations based on real data show that the proposed solution can notably reduce the convergence time compared to the state of the art without compromising the quality of the trained model.

papers.title: MEO: Mining Reliable Expert Signals for Offline Reinforcement Learning in Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: The operation of next-generation wireless networks increasingly hinges on Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to optimize critical network decisions. Offline RL trains agents using accessible datasets and thus eliminates costly online interactions, rendering it particularly advantageous in dynamic wireless environments that demand low latency and high safety. However, its capability remains under-explored in wireless settings, where offline data are often limited and subject to partial observability. As a result, the learned policy fails to fully capture the informative decision patterns hidden in the dataset. To bridge this gap, we propose MEO, a framework that mines reliable expert signals from wireless datasets for offline RL deployment. MEO first identifies reliable expert samples from imperfect offline data, and then learns a structured latent representation to better distinguish expert and non-expert behaviors. Based on the representation, MEO further derives a compensable reward signal that helps offline RL algorithms more effectively exploit valuable expert knowledge. We evaluate MEO in three practical wireless network scenarios using datasets collected from real-world deployments. The results show that MEO consistently outperforms existing methods across all three scenarios. Notably, MEO can be seamlessly integrated with any offline RL algorithms, highlighting its generalizability and potential for wide adoption in wireless networks. (Code is available at https://github.com/lpzu/MEO)

papers.title: Shapley Values for Modality Attribution in Robust Multimodal Remote Sensing Models
papers.abstract: Earth Observation models increasingly combine several data sources, yet it is often unclear how much each one contributes to the predictions of a given model on a given task. Quantifying these task-specific contributions is essential for interpreting multimodal models, diagnosing their reliance on individual inputs, and guiding the choice of data sources for a given application. We propose a principled framework for modality attribution based on exact Shapley values, enabled by recent multimodal architectures that are robust to missing modalities at inference time. Computing Shapley values requires evaluating model performance over all possible subsets of input modalities, which has forced previous work to resort to approximations or surrogate imputations. By leveraging such missing-modality-robust architectures, we instead compute exact Shapley values as originally defined. We showcase our approach on the CropHarvest dataset, a global binary crop-classification benchmark combining Sentinel-2, Sentinel-1, ERA5, and digital elevation data. Using two recent modality-fusion models, we evaluate all 2 4 modality coalitions to analyze modality importance at both global and local scales. Global Shapley values identify Sentinel-2 as the dominant modality, a finding further corroborated through a sensitivity analysis under two degradation regimes: additive Gaussian noise and simulated cloud-induced missing acquisitions. We further generate local Shapley attribution maps over 69,800 globally distributed test samples, revealing geographically structured patterns in modality contributions. Although demonstrated on a specific Earth Observation task, our framework is task-agnostic and even extends readily to multimodal learning problems in other domains.

papers.title: Hybridization of conceptual modeling and agent-based simulation in a context of climate change-related crisis management [résumé]
papers.abstract: The increased frequency and complexity of crises due to climate change make crisis management increasingly dependenton the ability to anticipate the consequences of decisions in dynamic and uncertain environments, particularly for threatenedpopulations. Decision-support systems can assist crisis stakeholders by structuring available information into a CommonOperational Picture (COP), identifying potential courses of action, and supporting operational planning (Barthe-Delanoëet al. 2025). However, such systems generally rely on conceptual representations of situations and actions, which maynot fully capture the emergent and unpredictable behavior of populations during a crisis. Agent-based simulation offers acomplementary perspective by explicitly representing individuals and their interactions, making it possible to explore howsituations evolve and populations react to interventions (Carles et al. 2025).Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) and Agent-Based Modeling and Simulation (ABMS) provide complementary approachesto representing complex systems. MDE uses models as primary artifacts to structure domain knowledge at different lev-els of abstraction and transform it into more concrete representations. ABMS represents systems through autonomous andheterogeneous agents whose interactions can generate emergent behavior. Their hybridization can therefore combine struc-tured and operational knowledge with the ability to explore its dynamic and emergent consequences. In crisis management,conceptual models can represent situations, actors, constraints, and intended actions, while agent-based models can explorehow these elements evolve through interactions between individuals and their environment. This creates a feedback processin which situational awareness guides simulation, while simulation results provide information for revising the conceptualrepresentation and subsequent decisions.To explore and assess this approach, we use two software programs implementing these paradigms: R-IO Suite1, a decision-support software designed to represent crisis situations and stakeholder actions according to a defined operational framework(Congès et al. 2024), and GAMA, an agent-based simulation platform. Their combination is investigated as a means ofimproving the preparation and adaptation of crisis management plans.Several conceptual and technical challenges have been identified. The first concerns the conceptual and semantic alignmentbetween the models used by R-IO Suite and GAMA. The second concerns differing temporalities, including discrete versuscontinuous time and synchronous versus asynchronous exchanges. The third relates to technical interoperability, while thefourth concerns computational performance and its impact on synchronization between the two systems.To investigate these challenges, several approaches to constructing the GAMA simulation are being considered. One pos-sibility is to develop a simulation of the crisis environment approaching a digital-analogue paradigm, where new data pro-gressively updates the simulated situation and enables exploration of its evolution under different conditions. Another is todevelop reusable simulation models that can be instantiated and parameterized according to the inferences and predictionsproduced by R-IO Suite. The choice between these approaches remains an open research question and may depend on thecrisis type, available data, and requirements of the decision-support process.

papers.title: Moov'Hanoi : design of a web-based architecture for operationalizing GAMA mobility simulations [résumé]
papers.abstract: Hanoi's mobility remains dominated by private vehicles, contributing to frequent congestion and traffic-related pollution.To reduce this dependence, the city is expanding its bus and metro infrastructure, with twelve metro lines planned by 2050.However, infrastructure alone cannot guarantee modal shift. Services must also provide coherent connections between buses,metro stations, and travellers' daily activities. Moov'Hanoi project addresses this context with a GAMA spatial agent-basedmodel that combines mobility and geographic data to assess public-transport reorganization, station accessibility, and traveland environmental indicators under different scenarios. However, using the model directly in GAMA platform requiresspecific knowledge to configure experiments and execute simulations, creating a barrier for stakeholders without GAMAexperience. A separate interaction layer could reduce this barrier while preserving GAMA as the simulation engine.Previous work, including the SIMPLE project, explored coupling GAMA simulations with Unity virtual-reality worlds,enabling exchange between model state and user actions. Whereas SIMPLE relies on a specialized VR environment, weinvestigate coupling through a standard web browser. The application connects to an already running GAMA server, loadsa configured model and experiment, and manages one active runtime instance. Users can then control simulation execution,manage execution mode, and observe spatial outputs. The architecture does not expose editing of the GAML specification,model parameters, GIS geometries, network topology, or agent behaviors.To realize this objective, we designed a three-component architecture containing a MapLibre GL JS browser client, a NestJSback-end, and GAMA server (figure 1). The browser provides simulation controls and spatial visualization. The back-endcoordinates the experiment lifecycle, retrieves model state, and distributes updates, while GAMA server executes the exper-iment. In terms of communication, the browser sends commands through HTTP, while Socket.IO delivers lifecycle events,cycle information, and dynamic spatial updates from the back-end. Between the back-end and GAMA server, the TypeScriptGAMA client library uses WebSocket to load the experiment, issue simulation commands, and retrieve model state. To makethis exchange reusable across models, a lightweight model-to-web contract uses GAML metadata to select, order, and classifyspecies. Static species, such as Moov'Hanoi's road and public-transport networks, are transferred during initialization, whiledynamic species, such as person agents, are retrieved periodically again during execution. This classification determineswhich spatial layers are refreshed. The retrieved geometries are rendered through point, line, and polygon layers.

papers.title: Towards Fair and Private Synthetic Health Data: A Hybrid Generative Framework under Zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: Machine learning for clinical prediction and decision support is constrained by limited, biased, and privacy-sensitive patients' data. While generative models offer a promising alternative, most fail to jointly ensure high utility, fairness, and formal privacy guarantees. This paper presents SF-GAN, a hybrid generative framework that integrates a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) with a Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) and an adversarial fairness mechanism. The CVAE captures complex feature dependencies in mixed-type clinical data through tailored reconstruction objectives and class-conditional generation, enabling improved handling of class imbalance. To ensure privacy, zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy (zCDP) is incorporated during CVAE training via gradient clipping and calibrated noise injection, providing rigorous privacy guarantees while preserving data fidelity. Building on these private representations, the WGAN-GP stage enhances sample realism and diversity through stable adversarial training. A dedicated fairness critic is introduced to predict sensitive attributes from generated samples, while the generator is trained to minimize this predictability, thereby enforcing statistical independence and reducing demographic bias. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that SF-GAN consistently outperforms baselines in predictive utility, fairness, and substantially reduces privacy risks. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of each component, and privacy-utility analyses show robustness across varying privacy budgets.

papers.title: Exploring Utility-Fairness-Privacy Trade-offs in Synthetic Sensitive Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Sharing sensitive tabular healthcare data requires generative models that balance the fundamentally conflicting objectives of statistical utility, demographic fairness, and individual privacy. Conventional configuration relies on scalarized search, which reduces this multidimensional tension to a single score and returns a single operating point, leaving the broader trade-off landscape unexplored. We introduce Evo-Clust-VAE-WGAN-GP, a framework treating generative model configuration as a tri-objective optimization problem over structural and training hyperparameters using NSGA-II to approximate the Pareto front. Rather than a head-to-head optimizer contest, we conduct a landscape characterization study, using Simulated Annealing and Bayesian Optimization as scalarized reference probes to expose what single-point strategies structurally cannot access. Evaluating across five healthcare benchmarks (HIV, Stress, Obesity, Heart Failure, Pediatric), results show that scalarized probes consistently collapse onto dataset-insensitive regions. In contrast, evolutionary search uncovers well-distributed, dataset-dependent Pareto fronts ranging from continuous to fragmented. These findings demonstrate that a single configuration compromise cannot adequately represent generative model behavior, establishing population-based search as a principled framework for exposing the full trade-off landscape in privacy-sensitive data generation.

papers.title: ArchTopic - LLM-Enhanced Framework for Archival Topic Extraction and Thematic Clustering
papers.abstract: Concise topic tagging of individual records enhances searchability and supports targeted thematic analysis within large archival corpora. Aggregating these tags into higher-level representations enables macro-scale pattern discovery and user-centric navigation across heterogeneous historical datasets. To meet these objectives, we developed a three-stage computational framework named ArchTopic - LLM-Enhanced Framework for Archival Topic Extraction and Thematic Clustering. Stage 1 applies zero-shot prompting with the LLaMA 3.2 3B model for context-driven topic extraction. Stage 2 enforces semantic alignment between generated topics and source texts through multilingual embedding comparison, cosine-similarity thresholding, and iterative refinement via a dual-LLM ensemble. Stage 3 builds a higher-level representation of the entire corpus by concatenating validated text and topic embeddings, reducing dimensionality with UMAP for topology preservation, clustering with k-means determined by the elbow criterion, and labeling clusters using YAKE (Yet Another Keyword Extractor) augmented with LLM-guided label synthesis. Our evaluation of more than 180,000 administrative correspondence records (1581–1859) from the Portuguese Overseas Historical Archive (Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino), specifically the Collection of Conselho Ultramarino, shows that the proposed framework produces well-separated, semantically coherent clusters, while embedding-space visualizations and word-cloud analyses confirm thematic integrity. We validate the framework’s superior cluster distinctiveness, label coherence, and computational throughput through comparative benchmarks against traditional Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and BERTopic approaches. Integrated LLM prompting, embedding validation, and clustering algorithms together establish a reproducible, scalable framework for thematic exploration and intuitive navigation of extensive archival collections. papers.title: Protocol for Systematic Review: Adaptive Transformer Models for Streaming Anomaly Detection in Solar Microgrids
papers.abstract: This research addresses the challenge of real-time anomaly detection in solar microgrids, which operate in non-stationary environments where concept drift frequently occurs due to environmental variability and system changes. Traditional anomaly detection methods assume stationary data distributions and struggle in streaming contexts, leading to degraded performance. Purpose of the Research: The project proposes an adaptive transformer model for streaming anomaly detection in solar microgrids, designed to maintain detection accuracy under dynamic conditions while operating within edge constraints. The model integrates drift monitoring for online updates, employs sparse attention to reduce computational overhead, and supports interpretability through attention-based visualization for actionable operator insights. A systematic review of transformer-based models for streaming anomaly and fault detection in energy systems informs this work. The review evaluates how existing studies address drift adaptation, latency and memory constraints for edge deployment, and interpretability for operator action. It identifies gaps at the intersection of streaming, adaptation, edge efficiency, and interpretability, which justify the proposed solution. Expected Outcomes: 1. A practical adaptive transformer optimized for streaming anomaly detection in solar microgrids. 2. Theoretical insights into sustaining transformer performance under concept drift and efficiency constraints. 3. Improved operational reliability through faster fault identification and reduced maintenance overhead. This research advances real-time anomaly detection for energy systems by addressing adaptation, efficiency, and interpretability within a unified framework, contributing to sustainable energy access and resilience.

papers.title: Beyond the digital divide: algorithmic marginalisation in the age of AI
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to examine how the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) may exacerbate the existing digital divide and create new forms of inequality, particularly among marginalised communities. Drawing on the Matthew effect, the paper explores how existing advantages in digital access, AI literacy and knowledge resources may accumulate over time, enabling privileged groups to benefit disproportionately from AI while further disadvantaging those already excluded. Design/methodology/approach This paper adopts a qualitative, conceptual methodology based on a critical review of the literature on the digital divide, digital equity, AI literacy and the Matthew effect. It also uses a conceptual figure to illustrate how AI-driven decisions, shaped by information available in online data sets, may be imposed on marginalised communities whose experiences and perspectives remain underrepresented in these data sets. Findings AI may deepen existing inequalities when digital data sets underrepresent the knowledge and experiences of marginalised communities. The Gujjar and Bakerwal communities of Jammu and Kashmir illustrate how such omissions can exclude them from AI-driven decision-making. Digital equity must therefore ensure not only access to technology but also meaningful representation in the knowledge systems shaping otherwise AI risks reinforcing the very inequalities it promises to overcome. Originality/value This paper is original and represents the authors’ own work. It offers a distinct perspective on the relationship between AI, the digital divide and the marginalisation of underrepresented communities.

papers.title: Uncovering themes in user reviews of a smart urban mobility application with BERTopic: a data-driven framework for service improvement
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to identify the thematic structure of long-form user feedback on a smart urban mobility application in Istanbul by analyzing user reviews and to translate these themes into actionable insights for service improvement. Design/methodology/approach A total of 10,000 user reviews of the Istanbulkart – Dijital Hesabim application, posted on the Google Play Store between June 2019 and April 2025, were analyzed using BERTopic, which combines transformer-based contextual embeddings with density-based clustering and a class-based TF-IDF representation. The topics were then consolidated into themes and interpreted qualitatively. Findings The model extracted 40 topics, consolidated into six themes: transportation card integration issues, technical performance and application stability, payment systems and financial transactions, authentication and security, identity verification and account recovery, and general satisfaction and criticism. Transportation card integration problems formed the largest topic (13.21% of the 5,406 classified reviews), indicating that the transition between physical and digital systems remains the most salient difficulty in these reviews. Research limitations/implications The corpus, in which dissatisfied users are over-represented, comprises long-form Android reviews of a single application, so the findings describe what these users report and have limited generalizability. Irony and emojis remain difficult to interpret. Practical implications Findings from long-form reviews give local authorities and developers a starting point for prioritizing improvements in application stability, authentication and card integration. Originality/value The study shows that topic share alone is a misleading basis for prioritization, since the most frequent theme is the least severely rated and the problem profile shifts markedly across application versions.

papers.title: Een datagedreven blik op de arbeidsmarkt: verklaarbare machine learning voor aanbod, vraag en vaardigheden
papers.abstract: Public employment services (PES) increasingly deploy machine learning (ML) to target scarce resources, yet the opacity of these models limits their comprehensibility, actionability and uptake in high-stakes decision-making. This dissertation examines how interpretable ML applied to large-scale administrative and online job vacancy (OJV) data of the Flemish PES (VDAB) can help address labor market matching inefficiencies across the supply, demand and skills dimensions, and what the findings imply for the design of interpretable decision support systems (iDSS). Study 1 compared TreeSHAP and TreeInterpreter on an eight-metric evaluation framework for VDAB's deployed Random Forest profiling model. A computationally efficient approximation preserved explanatory quality, which makes real-time explanations feasible at scale. Study 2 developed an ML framework for predicting hard-to-fill vacancies. XGBoost performed best, the XAI method SHAP identified vacancy text and company embeddings as key predictors, and counterfactual explanations (CF-SHAP) yielded actionable recommendations for recruitment. Study 3 benchmarked Markov Stability community detection on a co-occurrence graph, k-means on transformer-based embeddings and a contrastive graph neural network for clustering skills demanded in vacancies, and evaluated the solutions through internal validation metrics and stakeholder assessments. No paradigm dominated, semantic similarity and vacancy co-occurrence proved empirically dissociable signals of skill relatedness, and internal metrics aligned poorly with perceived utility. Across studies, adverse labor market outcomes showed meaningful predictability, particularly when models accommodated non-linear relationships. Prior unemployment and vacancy durations emerged as consistently strong predictors on both sides of the market, while behavioral platform traces, vacancy texts and company embeddings captured dimensions that conventional variables leave unobserved. Local explanations further revealed non-linear, interaction and context-dependent effects that aggregate analyses obscure, which supports individualized assessment and the formulation of new hypotheses. Data-driven skill taxonomies required expert involvement to reach operational quality. The dissertation synthesizes the studies into a four-layer framework for PES decision support, consisting of detection, diagnosis, actionable recourse and skills infrastructure, and discusses the trade-offs between predictive utility, diagnostic intelligence and actionability that arise in its design and use.

papers.title: Building Intelligent Ethical Governance in the AI Era through AI-Based Prophetic Leadership for Institutional Transformation
papers.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has accelerated institutional transformation through data analysis capabilities, process automation, and technology-based decision-making support. However, the increasing use of AI also presents ethical challenges related to transparency, accountability, algorithmic bias, and human responsibility in controlling technology. This study aims to explore how AI-Enabled Prophetic Leadership contributes to building Smart Ethical Governance to support sustainable institutional transformation. This study uses an exploratory qualitative approach involving 24 participants from three institutions that have implemented AI-based digital transformation. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation, and document analysis, then analyzed using thematic analysis techniques. The results of the study show three main findings, namely: (1) the reconstruction of prophetic leadership values (shiddiq, amanah, tabligh, and fathanah) into dimensions of digital integrity, moral accountability, communicative transparency, and ethical intelligence; (2) the integration of prophetic leadership and AI through human-centered decision-making, algorithmic oversight, system transparency, and strengthening organizational competencies; and (3) institutional transformation through structural, cultural, and operational changes. This research produces a conceptual model of the AI-Based Prophetic Ethical Governance Model (APEGM) that positions prophetic leadership as the foundation of values, AI as a decision-support instrument, and human oversight as a technology control mechanism. This research provides theoretical contributions to the development of ethical leadership and AI governance studies and provides practical implications for institutions in building innovative, responsible, and human-value-oriented digital transformations.

Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation, and document analysis, then analyzed using thematic analysis techniques. The results of the study show three main findings, namely: (1) the reconstruction of prophetic leadership values (shiddiq, amanah, tabligh, and fathanah) into dimensions of digital integrity, moral accountability, communicative transparency, and ethical intelligence; (2) the integration of prophetic leadership and AI through human-centered decision-making, algorithmic oversight, system transparency, and strengthening organizational competencies; and (3) institutional transformation through structural, cultural, and operational changes. papers.title: Perbandingan Ketahanan Lintas-Domain Indobert dan SVM Pada Ulasan Game dan Media Sosial Berbahasa Indonesia
papers.abstract: Sentiment classifiers for Indonesian app reviews are rarely tested on any app other than the one that provided their training data. This study contrasts a linear support vector machine (SVM) with TF-IDF features and a fine-tuned IndoBERT. Both models were trained on Roblox reviews and then tested on held-out Roblox reviews as well as on Minecraft and TikTok reviews from Google Play. Each app contributed 2,500 class-balanced reviews, with labels derived from ratings. Performance was measured by macro-F1 with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, and domain distance was assessed using five measures. On Roblox itself, IndoBERT and SVM showed no clear difference (0.867 vs 0.850). Across domains, IndoBERT scored roughly 0.065 higher and lost about 0.048 less. TikTok lay farther from Roblox on every distance measure and suffered larger drops, which is consistent with a distance effect. Domain-adaptive pretraining reduced the TikTok drop by 0.020 (macro-F1 rose from 0.794 to 0.810) but had no effect on Minecraft. In practical terms, IndoBERT is the safer option for developers who apply a classifier to other apps, while SVM is enough as a cheap in-domain baseline.

papers.title: Perbandingan IndoBERT dan mBERT Untuk Klasifikasi Toksisitas Pada Chat Roblox dan Minecraft Berbahasa Indonesia
papers.abstract: Toxic chat in online games exposes young players to harassment, while moderation of Indonesian chat is hampered by slang and non-standard spelling. This study compares monolingual IndoBERT and multilingual mBERT for four-class toxicity classification (neutral, violence, racist, harassment) of Indonesian Roblox and Minecraft chat to identify the more suitable model for moderation. Both models were fine-tuned with identical settings on the Indonesian Chat Dataset (10,702 chats) using three seeds, and evaluated with accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall, F1-score, and McNemar’s test. IndoBERT reached a mean macro F1-score of 0.8541 ± 0.0019 versus 0.8263 ± 0.0090 for mBERT, significant in two of three seeds. Neutral was the hardest class, and IndoBERT let 5.8% of toxic chats pass as neutral versus 8.3% for mBERT. Excluding 106 duplicated test chats did not change the ranking. Under these settings, IndoBERT performed better, although labels lack inter-annotator agreement and data cover two games only.

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Artificial Intelligence Governance Patterns in Selected Countries
papers.abstract: This study employs a comparative qualitative approach to analyze AI governance patterns in seven countries (Iran, the US, China, the EU, the UK, Japan, and Singapore). Data from official documents and academic sources were analyzed across five dimensions: policy focus, regulatory approach, ethical principles, technological infrastructure, and international cooperation. The findings identify three dominant patterns: 1) State-centered (China, Singapore), emphasizing central control and large-scale investment; 2) Market-based (US), relying on decentralized innovation and voluntary standards; and 3) Participatory-rights-based (EU, UK), featuring a risk-based approach with a focus on transparency and algorithmic justice. Japan focuses on solving social challenges through voluntary innovation. Despite institutional advances, Iran faces obstacles such as sanctions and structural inconsistencies. The conclusion underscores the need for a hybrid model tailored to Iran, integrating the EU's risk-based approach, Singapore's institutional coordination, and the localization of Islamic values. Policy recommendations include developing binding ethical codes, committing to long-term investment in indigenous infrastructure, and leading regional coalitions.

papers.title: Mitigating representation bias through constrained optimization
papers.abstract: Automated decision systems increasingly rely on people-related data, possibly amplifying discrimination already present in the real world. To prevent this, discrimination should be controlled throughout the data processing pipeline rather than assessed only on the final outcome. It may originate either from the data itself (representation bias) or from the algorithms that process the data (algorithmic bias), and can be characterized through properties such as coverage, which ensures sufficient representation of each protected group in the data, and fairness, which limits disparities among protected groups. This thesis focuses on data transformation, the preparation step in which a dataset is reshaped before analysis. This step deserves particular attention since it can amplify representation bias and propagate it to subsequent processing stages. This work investigates query rewriting as a way of correcting such bias. Given a selection query whose result violates a set of discrimination-aware constraints, the objective is to derive an alternative query that satisfies them while departing as little as possible from the original, thus preserving the analyst’s intent and the transparency of the transformation. Most existing query rewriting techniques address only one discrimination-related constraint at a time, enforcing either coverage or fairness over the query result, but not both simultaneously. To overcome this limitation, an initial optimization framework was proposed to jointly enforce coverage and fairness while minimizing deviation from the original query through a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) formulation. Its experimental evaluation, however, revealed scalability limitations, motivating the development of new optimization approaches. Building on this initial framework, this thesis first provides an extensive experimental investigation of the MINLP-based approach and then introduces a continuous reformulation of the query rewriting problem. The new model operates directly on the query selection constants, eliminating the discretized search space and enabling more scalable optimization techniques. The resulting problem is solved using a Differential Evolution-based approach. The two formulations are evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets and compared with state-of-the-art techniques under three settings: coverage constraints, fairness constraints, and their joint enforcement. The experimental results show a better trade-off among effectiveness, efficiency, and rewriting quality compared to the considered baseline approaches. Moreover, both formulations support the joint enforcement of coverage and fairness constraints, a setting not addressed by existing query rewriting techniques.

papers.title: A Full-Form Lexicon for Arabic Dialects Supporting Arabic NLP and Speech Technology
papers.abstract: Arabic dialects pose a distinctive challenge for lexical resources: they are acquired natively and used primarily in speech, while lacking a standard orthography. This paper presents DiaLEX, a family of large-scale full-form lexicons for six Arabic dialects (Egyptian, Hijazi, Emirati, Syrian, Lebanese, and Palestinian), comprising approximately 220 million entries, or an estimated 880 million if proclitics are enumerated. Unlike conventional dictionaries, DiaLEX exhaustively covers inflected, conjugated, cliticized, and negated wordforms, generated by a rule-based templatic framework validated by native-speaker linguists. Each entry carries a rich set of morphological, phonetic, and orthographic attributes. This paper (1)~examines DiaLEX's layered representation, which pairs a variant-rich Arabic-script layer with DARS, a primarily phonemic romanization tuned for speech technology; (2)~describes the generation methods, illustrated by Palestinian Arabic; and (3)~compares DiaLEX with existing dialectal resources, particularly MADAR/CODA. Applications to speech technology, machine translation, morphological analysis, and vocalization are discussed.

papers.title: The concept of financial models for scaling artificial intelligence systems for development and security
papers.abstract: Subject. The concept of financial models for scaling artificial intelligence (AI) systems in the context of development and security. Objectives. Suggest and justify new financial models for scaling AI systems that provide companies and organizations with safe development and effective investment in AI technologies. Methods. An interdisciplinary approach is applied, combining elements of risk management theory, AI economics, and security studies. Results. The challenges and risks associated with the process of scaling AI systems are detailed. The Comprehensive System for Secure Scaling of AI Systems is proposed and argued. The specific features of financial planning for the secure scaling of AI systems are substantiated. Based on existing financial mechanisms, alternative models of this process are proposed. Methods for evaluating the efficiency of investments in this process are identified and grouped by functional criterion. Conclusions and Relevance. The concept of financial models for the secure scaling of AI systems, as a comprehensive and multi-level approach, is essential for expanding the practical capabilities of AI and guaranteeing its security, ethics, and sustainability. The proposed security system encompasses risk management, continuous monitoring, and adaptation of advanced technologies. Evaluating the efficiency of investments in the secure scaling of AI systems goes beyond traditional financial metrics and therefore requires consideration of quantitative and qualitative aspects, economic benefits, innovation potential, competitiveness, pricing, and ethical factors. The results can be applied in managing resources and capital when scaling AI platforms, assessing related financial risks, ensuring security, as well as in developing regulatory frameworks and attracting investments.
